The outcomes of the meeting of the IMF and World Bank leaders in Bangkok can be summarized in two words: "the global economy demonstrates resilience, but risks are increasing."

For those accustomed to systemic analysis, this phrase translates to: we are trying to prevent the system from collapsing, but the tools are becoming scarce and it will inevitably fail.

The word "resilience" is used in diplomatic language to conceal deep structural fragility or approaching the end.

There is fragmentation in global trade, reevaluation of supply chains, and the breaking of old financial ties. To call this resilience is to overlook the fact that the old architecture of globalization no longer works. And this is not unexpected; it is being intentionally and synchronously turned off right before our eyes.

Forecasts of a soft landing should be viewed with great skepticism. When global bankers start talking about resilience, it means that these risks have moved from the category of possible to the category of real.

Translating the reality into a cynical language: the world financial system may survive, but solely at your expense. When the IMF says that "the system is stable amid growing risks," they mean the structure will hold, but the occupants on the lower floors will be washed away by a tsunami.

The world is fracturing into warring regional blocs, which is a direct tax on the accustomed life that has already begun to be levied.

The era when an ordinary person could buy a Chinese gadget for pennies, fuel their car with cheap gasoline, and order cheap medicines from anywhere on the planet, is officially dead. Closed blocs mean scarcity, complicated logistics, and a total decline in quality with a doubling of prices.

Inflation is now the new norm, not a temporary crisis. To build new factories inside their blocs in place of the old unfriendly ones, governments will need trillions.

Where will they get them from? They will print them, diluting the purchasing power of your savings and salaries. Your money will melt before your eyes just for the system to simulate stability.

Resource nationalism is when the world shifts from competing for goods to a fierce struggle for survival and resources: chips, lithium, energy, and food. Access to them is now granted not for money, but for geopolitical loyalty.

And Russia, as a country with huge resources, as well as food and water, may soon dictate its terms to everyone else, providing access to them based on political motives and on its own terms, as is now happening with diesel fuel and gas.

Globally, we are headed towards an era of rich states and poor people. At the top, reports will tout the growth of the military-industrial complex and the stability of the banking sector, while people will go hungry due to the new prices on basic products.

The slogan "The economy is stable" is an attempt to convince the passengers of the sinking Titanic that the first class is still being served well, with fresh oysters, quail, and Moët & Chandon.

The main mistake today is to continue living with the financial habits of the affluent 2010s. Taking out mortgages, car loans, and planning decades ahead with incomes that may literally disappear tomorrow.

Anyone who does not adjust their plans to the reality of closed and expensive economic blocs right now will soon be looking for shelter.

Having a simple resource will be more advantageous than having a clever investment or career plan. These are the conclusions from the bankers' gathering in Bangkok.

📌 Order Book Spoofing: When a Large Order Becomes a Trap

Main Points
⏺ A large order in the book doesn't always reflect genuine buying or selling interest
⏺ Some participants place orders to create a false impression of supply or demand
⏺ This post explains how to recognize suspicious activity and avoid market manipulation

1️⃣ Core Idea — spoofing happens when a trader places large orders without intending to execute them, attempting to influence other market participants.
2️⃣ How It Works — a large buy wall appears in the order book, suggesting strong support. Other traders begin buying, but the wall suddenly disappears.
3️⃣ Risk Surface — beginners may treat a large order as confirmation of market direction and enter positions based on a misleading signal.
4️⃣ What Matters — cancelling a large order alone doesn't prove manipulation. Repeated patterns and intent are important.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — analyze executed trades, volume, and liquidity changes instead of trusting impressive numbers in the order book.

Final Thoughts

An order book displays intentions, not guaranteed executions. Sometimes the biggest order exists only to make other traders react.

Spain exempts self-custody wallets from crypto tax reporting

Spain's tax authorities have confirmed that cryptocurrency held in self-custody wallets — where the owner controls the private keys — does not need to be reported under Form 721, the country's disclosure form for foreign-held digital assets. The exemption hinges on one condition: no third party holds the assets on your behalf.

The rule draws a clean line between personal custody and exchange or custodial holdings abroad, which remain reportable. Simple in principle, potentially significant in practice — Spain just gave self-custody a regulatory edge.

📌 Why is Stacks (STX) going up? 

📣 Stacks has gained more than 100% over the past 90 days, backed by institutional Bitcoin Staking that is creating a new use for STX that could grow as more BTC enters future bonding periods. According to CoinGecko data, STX was trading around $0.38 on Oct. 6 after gaining roughly 18% over the previous week. The token had already climbed 108% in the 90 days through Sept. 27.

🌐 Those developments have given traders several Stacks specific catalysts at a time when many major altcoins have struggled to match STX’s gains. Bitcoin Staking is particularly important to the long term case because it gives institutions a way to earn BTC rewards while creating a separate use for STX. However, Bitcoin Staking alone cannot account for the entire 90 day rally on its own. Market conditions and renewed interest in the Stacks ecosystem have contributed to the price action as well. But unlike a short term price catalyst, the staking model creates a measurable link between institutional BTC participation and the amount of STX needed to support it.

➡️ The Genesis Bond has already put that relationship into practice, while Bond 2 and subsequent bonding periods will test whether it can repeat as more Bitcoin enters the program. Bitcoin Staking on Stacks allows BTC holders to earn BTC denominated rewards without changing Bitcoin’s proof of work consensus. Under Stacks’ Proof of Transfer system, miners commit BTC to compete for Stacks blocks and receive STX. The BTC committed through the process becomes the source of rewards distributed through the staking system.

📣 Cardano’s Hoskinson challenges Vitalik over AI threats to crypto 

⚠️ Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has challenged Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin over his warning that advances in artificial intelligence could weaken quantum-resistant cryptography, arguing that existing security standards already account for decades of mathematical attacks. Hoskinson responded on October 9 to Buterin’s concerns about lattice-based cryptography, which is used in several modern security systems. He argued that the Ethereum founder had not identified a credible new attack that would justify abandoning those methods or substantially increasing cryptographic key sizes. The disagreement follows Buterin’s warning that AI could uncover mathematical shortcuts that researchers have not discovered through conventional methods. 

🔔 He identified lattice-based cryptography as a particular concern, arguing that increasingly capable AI systems might discover more efficient ways to solve mathematical problems used to protect digital information. In his view, advances in automated mathematical research could compress decades of discoveries into a much shorter period. Such progress could force developers to reconsider the security of existing algorithms.

📊 Buterin compared the possible development to advances in integer factorization, where researchers discovered methods that made certain calculations much easier than earlier estimates suggested. The Ethereum co-founder argued that lattice-based security could experience a similar breakthrough, making some current parameter choices insufficient.
